name: Premolar extraction orthodontics

card.summary: Removing usually four premolars during braces to align crowded or protruding teeth, which can retract the lips and change profile; the effect on midface look is debated in orthodontics and looksmaxxing circles.
card.aka: Teeth extraction for facial change; four-premolar extraction; extraction orthodontics
card.note: Extraction is irreversible; looksmaxxing forums include members reporting regret and discussing later expansion and implant work.

quick.overview:
In orthodontics, premolars (the teeth between canines and molars) are sometimes extracted to create room for crowded teeth or to pull back protruding front teeth. For appearance, the intended gains are straighter teeth and, in convex-profile patients, a softer lip profile.

Looksmaxxing communities focus on the opposite worry: that extraction narrows the arch and reduces forward support of the lips and midface, giving a flatter or dished-in look. Meta-analyses find extraction is linked with lip retraction and a more upright profile on average, with very low-certainty evidence and large variation between cases.
quick.how: A treating orthodontist plans extraction from crowding, overjet, profile and growth pattern, removes the teeth (commonly four first premolars), then closes the spaces with fixed braces or aligners over a treatment course of about two years. Some clinicians start borderline cases without extraction and re-assess. Some patients seek second opinions on non-extraction approaches such as expansion.
quick.risks: Extracted teeth do not grow back. Reviews report narrower molar widths after extraction, and observational literature raises questions about relapse of lower crowding and root resorption with braces generally. Online accounts describe regret over narrow arches and perceived midface changes, with some pursuing expansion surgery and implants.

lead: Premolar extraction in orthodontics is the removal of premolars, most often four first premolars, to resolve dental crowding or to create room to retract protruding front teeth during fixed-appliance treatment [1][2]. Orthodontists see it as one of several treatment options chosen according to crowding, space needs, overjet, torque and facial aesthetics [3].

The practice sits at the center of a long-running debate in orthodontics. Opponents argue that removing premolars produces a concave profile with poor lip support, while others report that the soft-tissue effect depends on the starting profile and that flattening with age occurs in extraction and non-extraction patients alike [3]. Extraction rates have declined over time, which a clinician writing in Dentistry attributes partly to practitioner preference and partly to public opinion and social-media horror stories [3].

In looksmaxxing forums, the topic is discussed as a risk to forward growth and midface projection, particularly in teenagers still growing [4][5]. Systematic reviews of fixed-appliance patients report lip retraction and a more upright profile on average after extraction, with the quality of evidence rated very low [6][7].

chain: Straighter smile and, in some patients, less lip protrusion
angle.text: Orthodontists use extraction to align crowded teeth and, in patients with protruding teeth, to reduce lip fullness and convexity of the profile. People concerned with midface projection discuss whether the same space closure can reduce lip support, which is why many seek non-extraction options or a second opinion.

paras: Orthodontists decide on extraction by assessing crowding, space requirement, overjet, torque and facial aesthetics, and some start borderline cases without extraction with a therapeutic diagnosis, accepting that extraction may be needed after initial alignment [3]. A 2023 review on asymmetric extraction notes the decision is also used where there is a significant midline discrepancy or lack of facial harmony [8].

After extraction, spaces are closed by retracting front teeth, often with anchorage aids such as mini-implants; reviews describe anterior en masse retraction as a standard approach [9]. Clear aligners have also been used in extraction cases, and a systematic review compared them with fixed appliances for complex cases [10].

A 2018 meta-analysis of controlled studies found extraction was associated with greater lower-lip retraction (about 2 mm), upper-lip retraction (about 1.3 mm), a larger nasolabial angle (about 4 degrees) and increased profile pleasantness in a smaller subset, with the authors rating the quality of evidence very low [7].

A 2024 meta-analysis of 30 studies (29 retrospective, one randomized) found maxillary and mandibular inter-first-molar width decreased by about 2 mm with four first-premolar extraction, mandibular intercanine width increased slightly more in the non-extraction group, and treatment was somewhat shorter without extraction [6]. A 2023 retrospective study of 77 adults found no significant difference in soft-tissue aesthetics among non-extraction, two-extraction and four-extraction groups, and its authors state that well-controlled incisor torque helps preserve soft-tissue aesthetics [11].

A long-term study of 63 borderline Class II patients compared extraction and non-extraction edgewise treatment after an average of 14.5 years, using cephalograms, models and a self-evaluation of esthetic impact [12]. Commentators cited in the Dentistry article note that in well-planned cases even dental professionals could not tell from profile alone whether extractions had been done [3].

The 2024 Angle Orthodontist meta-analysis and the 2018 European Journal of Oral Sciences meta-analysis are the main syntheses, and both rely largely on non-randomized comparisons [6][7]. Randomized trials in the extraction area mostly test how to speed tooth movement after extraction, for example low-intensity electrical current, photobiomodulation, piezocision and micro-osteoperforation [13][14][15][16].

Registered trials include comparisons of premolar extraction with distalization in Class II patients, studies of root resorption, and an effect on vertical facial dimension [17][18][19]. A cross-sectional NHANES analysis examined sleep disruption and premolar absence, and a 2023 study examined mandibular kinematics after premolar extraction [20][21].

Long-term follow-up of four-premolar extraction cases found lower anterior crowding continued to increase between 10 and 20 years after retention, with only about 10 percent of cases judged clinically acceptable at the last stage [22]. An earlier 65-case study found long-term response was unpredictable [23]. Root resorption has been examined as a treatment-related risk in a series of 868 fixed-appliance patients [24].

On looksmax.org, a 16-year-old asked whether extraction for crowding would harm forward growth while in treatment with a palate expander [4]. Another user who had four premolars removed years earlier described a narrow palate and recessed maxilla and asked about reversal; a reply suggested surgical expansion followed by implants to fill spaces, noting the cost [5]. A community-maintained list of clinicians who treat what members call premolar extraction/retraction sufferers also circulates [25].

timeline.event: Study of 65 first-premolar extraction cases reports unpredictable long-term lower alignment [23].
Long-term comparison of extraction and non-extraction therapy in borderline Class II patients published [12].
Meta-analysis of soft-tissue changes after extraction published [7].
Retrospective study of 77 adults finds no significant soft-tissue aesthetic difference among groups [11].
Meta-analysis of 30 studies compares extraction and non-extraction outcomes [6].

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing posts frame premolar extraction as a possible cause of lost midface projection and narrow arches, often alongside expansion treatments [4][5].

claims.claim: Extraction during growth can reduce forward midface development
claims.believers: Teen patients and parents on looksmax.org ask whether extraction harms forward growth and midface projection [4].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report lip retraction and narrower molar width after extraction, and attribute profile flattening in both groups partly to maturation [3][6][7].

claims.claim: The effects can be reversed with expansion surgery and implants
claims.believers: Forum replies describe surgically assisted expansion followed by implants as a route, at high cost [5].
claims.experts: No trials of this reversal approach are cited in the reviewed literature.
